prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

on a line from Szymborska My departure from the city of O.? I took no leave. I’d learned to sleep angry. On a train I was contained. The water under the bridge was just that. Shunned metaphor. It did not send waves of regret or make me reflect. It did not baptize, wash away, or cleanse. The countryside appeared like the sides of any country where rain falls and cows chew yellow flowers. The world was not too much or too much with me. I stomached it. In the photograph I only look lonely because I was alone. You cannot see the envelope on my lap or the letters lodged under sweaters in my suitcase. I carried only one bag, what I could manage in a crowd. You can imagine I held a thick book from which nothing could distract me. You can imagine my head high, eyes dry. I did not see my departure as a failure, or a fall. I’d dodged a bullet. Been reborn. You can imagine it that way. Only none of it was like that, not like that at all.

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your poem, with refined phrasing and rhythm while preserving its original imagery, structure, and emotional restraint:

---

*after a line from Szymborska*

My departure from the city of O.—did I take my leave? I had learned, instead, to sleep with my anger. On the train, I was contained. The water beneath the bridge was only that: water. I refused its metaphor. It summoned no waves of regret, provoked no reflection. It did not baptize, did not wash away, did not cleanse.

The countryside unfolded as countryside does—rain falling, cows grazing on yellow flowers, indistinguishable from any other. The world was neither too much, nor too much with me. I simply bore it.

In the photograph, I appear lonely only because I was alone. What the frame does not show: the envelope resting on my lap, the letters hidden beneath sweaters in my suitcase. I carried a single bag—only what I could manage through a crowd.

You might imagine I held a thick book, one from which nothing could distract me. You might imagine my head held high, my eyes dry. That I did not read my departure as failure, or as falling—but as a bullet dodged. A rebirth.

You may imagine it that way.

Only none of it was like that. Not like that at all.

---

I focused on smoothing transitions, tightening syntax, and elevating word choice (e.g., "unfolded," "bore," "summoned") while keeping the poem's deliberate flatness, its refusal of sentimentality, and its powerful closing reversal intact. Let me know if you'd like a version that leans more spare and minimalist, or one with even more lyrical elaboration.

---

after a line by Szymborska

There was no farewell when I left city O. I had mastered the art of sleeping while furious. The train held me together. Beneath the bridge, water remained simply water—I refused its symbolic weight. No swells of remorse rose up, no moment of introspection followed. Nothing was purified, rinsed clean, or made new by it.

The landscape unfolded like any rural stretch anywhere—rainfall, cattle grazing on yellow blossoms. The weight of existence didn't crush me; I managed to swallow it whole.

That photograph makes me appear solitary only because solitude was my actual state. What's invisible: the envelope resting on my knees, the letters tucked beneath sweaters in my luggage. I traveled light—a single bag, easy to manage among crowds.

Picture me, if you like, absorbed in some substantial novel, immune to distraction. Picture my chin lifted, my eyes clear of tears. I refused to frame my leaving as defeat or collapse. Perhaps I'd narrowly escaped disaster. Perhaps I'd emerged transformed.

You're welcome to imagine it this way.

But none of it happened like that. Not remotely.
outputs.L3:
I left the city of O. the way one leaves a room after an argument that never quite happened—quickly, quietly, without ceremony. There were no farewells, no lingering embraces on a platform, no last walks past familiar landmarks committed to memory for sentimental purposes. I simply went. The absence of ritual was not an oversight; it was, if anything, the only honest way to mark an ending that resisted being marked at all.

I want to say, clearly, that I have no interest in turning any of this into metaphor. The water I crossed was water, not some passage between one version of myself and another. The journey was a journey—hours passing, a body moving through space—not a pilgrimage, not an initiation. The countryside that blurred past the window was simply countryside: fields, fences, the occasional startled bird. I refuse to let it stand in for grief, or hope, or renewal. These things resist being made to mean something they were never asked to mean.

There is a photograph from that time, and it looks lonely. I understand why. A single figure, an empty platform, the flat light of early morning. But the loneliness is a trick of framing. Just outside the edges of that image were an envelope I had not yet opened and letters I had not yet read, tucked away, deliberately out of frame. The photograph shows a person alone; it does not show what that person was carrying, unopened, folded, weighing almost nothing and yet somehow impossible to set down. The stillness in the picture conceals rather than reveals.

I know how this could be told differently. I know the shapes such stories are supposed to take. Someone might imagine that I was fleeing danger, that I had narrowly escaped some catastrophe—dodging a bullet, as the saying goes. Someone else might prefer to see it as a kind of rebirth, a shedding of an old self on the far bank of that water, a triumphant arrival into a better, freer version of my life. These are satisfying shapes. They have beginnings, middles, and the promise of resolution. I understand their appeal.

But none of it happened that way. There was no danger to dodge, no rebirth waiting on the other side. There was only the leaving itself—plain, undramatic, and stripped of the narrative gestures that might have made it easier to carry. Whatever meaning exists in that departure is not the meaning of escape or transformation. It is something quieter and less accommodating, something that refuses, even now, to be resolved into a story anyone would choose to tell.
outputs.L4:
*Note: Since I don't have the specific poem text you're referencing, I'll expand this summary into a fuller literary analysis based on the interpretive framework you've provided. If you can share the actual poem, I can offer a more precise, textually-grounded reading.*

---

The poem opens with what appears to be a straightforward act: a speaker leaving a city, boarding a train, watching the landscape recede. From the outset, the tone is flat, almost clinical. There is no lingering on doorframes, no backward glances weighted with meaning, no images of skylines dissolving into nostalgia. The speaker seems determined to strip the journey of any romantic or elegiac quality—refusing, in effect, the poetic conventions that typically accompany departure narratives. Trains have long served as vehicles (literally and figuratively) for reflection, transition, and metaphor: the rhythmic clatter of wheels mirroring a racing heart, windows framing scenes of loss, motion standing in for emotional transformation. This poem seems aware of that inheritance and actively resists it. The language remains plain, declarative, almost bureaucratic in its precision—describing timetables, platforms, the mechanics of sitting and waiting, rather than the interior weather of the person undergoing the experience.

This restraint reads, at first, as a form of control. The speaker's composure suggests someone who has processed whatever precipitated the departure, someone who can now recount it without being undone by it. The absence of tears, of dramatic gestures, of interior monologue spiraling into grief or anger, creates the impression of a person fully in command of their own narrative. We are meant to trust this account because of its very lack of embellishment; the plainness functions as a kind of rhetorical credibility, the way understatement often signals authenticity in confessional writing. The speaker seems to be saying: *I am not performing my pain for you. This is simply what happened.*

But the poem's final move dismantles this carefully built structure. In its closing lines, the speaker turns on the entire account just given, stating plainly: none of it was like that. This retraction does not merely add nuance—it detonates the preceding narrative altogether. Suddenly the reader must reconsider everything: the flat affect, the deliberate avoidance of metaphor, the composed recounting of departure. Were these simply omissions, or active falsifications? The poem suggests both. The controlled exterior we were given was not an accurate record filtered through restraint, but a fabrication—a story told *in place of* the real one, perhaps because the real one was too unwieldy, too devastating, or too resistant to language altogether.

This final admission reframes the poem's entire strategy. What had seemed like stoic understatement is revealed instead as a kind of protective fiction, a narrative armor constructed precisely because the truth could not be approached directly. The refusal of metaphor, we now understand, was not a rejection of sentimentality for its own sake, but a symptom of avoidance—an inability or unwillingness to access the emotional reality of the departure. The poem thus performs a double movement: it first offers a controlled, almost anesthetized version of leaving, then collapses that version entirely, exposing the artifice beneath it.

What remains, in the wake of this collapse, is absence rather than revelation. The poem does not replace the false narrative with a "true" one; it does not suddenly break into raw confession or unguarded feeling. Instead, it leaves a void where the real story might have been—an admission that the actual experience resists articulation, or that the speaker is still unable or unwilling to give it voice. This creates a profound tension between what is said and what is felt, between performance and authenticity. The poem ultimately becomes less about the act of leaving a city than about the impossibility of narrating emotional truth directly—about the gap that persists between composed language and the disordered, unspeakable interior life it fails to capture. In undercutting its own account, the poem enacts the very evasion it describes, leaving readers with not a resolved departure but an open wound disguised, until the final line, as calm.
outputs.L5:
# On the Shunned Muse: Wisława Szymborska's Quiet Rebellion

There is something quietly radical about Wisława Szymborska's decision to shun the grand gestures that poetry so often demands. In a century that produced manifestos, revolutions, and poets who saw themselves as prophets, she chose smallness. She chose doubt. She chose the onion, the cat in an empty apartment, the moment after catastrophe when someone must still sweep the streets.

Szymborska shunned certainty above all else. Her Nobel Prize acceptance speech, delivered in 1996, celebrated the phrase "I don't know" as the engine of all genuine creation. This was itself a kind of shunning—a rejection of the poet-as-oracle tradition that runs from the Romantics through much of twentieth-century verse. Where others sought to illuminate universal truths, she preferred to sit with particulars, to notice the strange fact of existence without rushing toward conclusions.

She also shunned the confessional mode that dominated so much postwar poetry. Her personal suffering—and she suffered, having lived through Nazi occupation and Stalinist Poland—rarely appears as raw autobiography. Instead, it gets refracted through irony, through historical distance, through the perspective of a stone or a cloud or a Renaissance painting. This shunning of direct emotional exposure was not coldness; it was a different kind of honesty, one that trusted indirection over confession.

Perhaps most tellingly, Szymborska shunned her own early work. The poems she wrote in the late 1940s and early 1950s, dutifully Stalinist in their politics, embarrassed her so thoroughly that she spent decades trying to prevent their republication. This act of self-shunning reveals something essential about her: a willingness to disown even her own words when they no longer matched her understanding of truth.

In shunning the expected, Szymborska found her particular genius—one built not on rejection for its own sake, but on the conviction that the overlooked, the small, and the uncertain deserved poetry's full attention.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free verse poem that begins with an epigraph line inspired by Wisława Szymborska, about leaving a city and rejecting the usual symbolism of rivers and rain.
counterfactuals.output:
*The river does not remember you, and rain has never once meant grief.*
—after Szymborska

I want to leave this city without the river doing anything
symbolic. It should just sit there, brown and practical,
carrying a plastic bag and half a bicycle wheel,
uninterested in my departure.

Let it rain if it wants to rain.
Weather is not obligated to comment on my life.
I refuse to stand at the window like a woman in a film,
translating drops into decades.

What actually happens when you leave a city:
you forget to cancel the gas.
You find a receipt from a restaurant
that closed two years ago and did not know it closed
until this moment, in your hand, folded like a small alibi.

The taxi driver asks where to
and you say the station, though you mean
something closer to *away from the shape
I have been standing in.*

No one should compare this to a river finding the sea.
Rivers don't find anything. They are pulled,
the way I am pulled, by grades of ground
too slow to notice, too old to argue with.

If it must rain, let it rain
on the ordinary things—
the bus shelter, the dropped glove,
a dog who did not ask to be out in this,
looking betrayed by the sky
for entirely dog-shaped reasons.

I am leaving because the lease is up.
I am leaving because a job appeared
in another postal code.
There is no metaphor doing the heavy lifting here,
only two suitcases and a friend who owes me forty dollars
I will probably not collect.

The city will not miss me
the way a poem misses its last line.
It will go on being a city—
indifferent, structural, full of people
hurrying past a river
that is only, ever, water
moving because water moves,
not because it means
to say goodbye.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a confessional poem about departure and denial, where the speaker insists water, rain, and countryside carry no metaphorical weight, ending with a twist that undercuts their own composure.
counterfactuals.output:
**Nothing But Weather**

I want to be clear: the rain that morning
meant nothing. It fell because clouds
had grown heavy, because pressure systems
collided somewhere over the interstate—
not because you were leaving,
not because I stood at the window
counting drops like some woman
in a poem about grief.

The water in the ditch was just water.
Brown, ordinary, full of last week's leaves.
I did not think of rivers that carry things away
and cannot be walked back into.
I did not think of anything
being carried away.

And the countryside you drove through—
those flat fields, that particular
shade of dying gold in October—
none of it was a correlative
for anything I felt. Grass is grass.
A silo is a silo, not a steeple,
not a marker, not the long white throat
of something trying to sing and failing.

I've read the books. I know
what writers do with weather,
how they dress the sky in feeling
until you can't tell the difference
between a storm and a heart
coming apart in a kitchen.
I refuse to do that. I insist
on the literal. The barometric.
The measurable inch of rain.

You left on a Tuesday.
It rained. The fields were the fields.
That's the whole of it, I swear—

except I keep standing at this window
every time it rains,
and I have started calling the sound
of water on the roof
your name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the voice of someone recalling leaving a place called "O.," resisting sentimentality, using plain imagery like trains, suitcases, and photographs, and ending with an ironic reversal.
counterfactuals.output:
# Leaving O.

I packed the suitcase in under an hour—
this took no courage, only arithmetic:
two shirts, the good coat, a photograph
I didn't look at twice before folding it
between socks so it wouldn't crease.

The station at O. was small, as stations go.
A single platform, a clock that ran three minutes slow,
which everyone accounted for
the way you learn to compensate
for a limp in someone you've always known.

I won't say the light did anything particular.
It was morning light, is all,
falling on the tracks the way it falls
on any tracks, in any town
with a name that fits on a sign.

The train came. I got on it.
Through the window O. did not
recede like a memory or ache
like something remembered—
it just got smaller, the way things do
when you're moving and they're not.

I didn't cry. I want that understood.
I ate the sandwich I had packed for the journey,
and it was a good sandwich, and I finished it
outside a town whose name I never learned,
and felt, for the first time in years,
entirely like myself—

which is to say: I have told you all of this
as though I left something behind in O.,
some truer version, tender and intact.

But the suitcase is still packed
the same way, in my new rooms.
The photograph still creases if you're careless.
And most mornings, standing at my window,
I find I am still waiting
for a train that's three minutes slow,
in a town I have not managed,
after all this time,
to leave.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a literary poem exploring self-deception during a personal departure—someone claiming calm and control while subtly revealing grief, referencing a nod to Szymborska’s style.
counterfactuals.output:
# Departure Protocol

I am fine, I tell the coffee cup,
the coat still warm on its hook,
the door that will not slam
because I am closing it so carefully,
like a woman defusing something.

See how steady my hands are
folding the same shirt three times.
See how I've made a list: *keys, charger, dignity*
and checked off everything but the last.

Wisława would say: forgive me, absence,
for calling you a Tuesday.
Forgive me, grief, for wearing
my most efficient shoes to meet you,
for scheduling you between
the packing and the leaving,
as though you were a dentist appointment,
as though you could be numbed.

I practice the sentence in the mirror—
*I'm simply ready for a change*—
until it sounds like weather,
like something that happens
to houses, not to hearts.

The plants I'm leaving get instructions,
precise as a will: *water Tuesdays,
morning light, don't overthink it*—
advice I cannot take myself.

I am so calm I could be furniture.
I am so calm the calm has a texture,
rough as the inside of a held breath.

Somewhere in the packing boxes
is the photograph I keep almost throwing out
and keep almost keeping,
that small failure of decisiveness
that says more than any letter—

how the average catastrophe
wears its Sunday clothes,
how the heart, that terrible amateur,
keeps confusing endings
with mere geography,

how I will stand in the doorway
one last practical minute,
checking the stove, the locks, the lights,
anything, anything
but the shape of what I'm holding
as I finally, calmly,
competently,
turn to go.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short narrative poem about leaving a town after a breakup or personal crisis, focusing on restrained emotion, unreliable narration, and a closing line that admits the opposite of everything just said.
counterfactuals.output:
**Leaving Millbrook**

I packed the car in twenty minutes flat,
which proves how little there was worth the keeping—
a coffee pot, three shirts, the cat
who never liked you anyway. No weeping,
I want that understood. I checked the gauge,
noted the tank was three-quarters full,
enough to clear the county without stopping.
The house looked smaller in the side mirror, the way
things do when you're glad to see them shrinking.

I took the long way past the diner, not
because I hoped you'd be out front like always
smoking on the step—I'd simply forgot
the shortcut, that's all, the roads this time of day's
maze of stop signs, calm suggestion. Fine.
The radio played something I didn't recognize
and I didn't turn it up or down. My hands
stayed steady on the wheel. This is a plain sign
of a man who's settled things, who understands
that towns are only towns, that leaving is
no different than any other Tuesday drive.

I did not look back at the water tower.
I did not think of the porch light left burning,
a small mistake, an oversight, an hour
I could've spent packing instead of turning
it off myself, the way I should have. No,
I drove until the exit signs turned strange,
until the names of towns meant nothing, and I felt
nothing, which is worth mentioning twice. So
I'll say it plain, so nothing's left to melt
or misconstrue: I am fine. I am not fine at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
